title: Culluloo Telewana Monument
summary: A stone monument in Woodsburgh remembers Culluloo Telewana and invites a closer look at the misleading idea of the “last” Native person.
address_label: Wood Lane and Keene Lane, Woodsburgh
listing_image_alt: Historic postcard showing the Culluloo stone monument in Woodmere, with its inscribed face and stepped base.
ancestral_territory_note: Rockaway history and public remembrance on Long Island’s southwestern shore.
why_this_matters: A monument can preserve a person’s name while repeating ideas that obscure a people’s survival. Reading this inscription critically makes room for both remembrance and the continuing lives of Native communities.
introduction_content:
The Culluloo monument stands on a small triangle at Wood and Keene lanes in Woodsburgh. Its inscription, dated 1888, records Abraham Hewlett’s remembrance of a man he knew in childhood.

The monument was first placed in Woodmere and later moved to Woodsburgh.

The 1888 Inscription

Here lived and died
Culluloo Telewana,
A.D.1818
the last of the Rockaway
Iriquois [sic] Indians
who was personally
known to me in my boyhood.
I, owning the land, have
erected this monument
to him and his tribe.
Abraham Hewlett,
1888

The base bears the name CULLULOO. Transcription: Smithsonian American Art Museum sculpture inventory. The inscription’s claim that Rockaway people vanished, and its identification of them as Iroquois, reflect Hewlett’s account. Rockaway people were Algonquian-speaking; Native communities and descendants remain part of Long Island today.
history_content:
Hewlett described Telewana as the last of the Rockaway people and labelled them Iroquois. The Valley Stream Historical Society explains that Rockaway people were Algonquian-speaking and challenges the idea that Native history ended with one person’s death.

The stone preserves Hewlett’s memory, but its language also reflects a widespread habit of describing Native people as vanishing. Native communities and their descendants continue to shape Long Island’s life and history.
whereintheworld_content: The monument is at the intersection of Wood and Keene lanes. Respect neighboring homes and traffic when viewing it.
